name: saegmuller-equatorial-telescope

views: Fig. 1 side elevation, partly in section
Fig. 3 detail section at the eyepiece end of the tube

assumptions: The patent drawing has no dimensions. The model is a desk-size personal refractor, not life size: the main tube is assumed 136 mm long and 24 mm across, and every other size follows the proportions of Fig. 1 or of typical 1880s-1900s portable equatorial refractors.

Fig. 1 cuts off the objective end of the tube and the lower pier. The objective cell, dew shield, turned pier, three-legged base with leveling screws and the counterweights are filled in from typical portable equatorials of the period.
The polar axis is set 40 degrees above the horizon (about the latitude of Washington, D.C.) on a latitude pivot; in the assembly the tube points 35 degrees up.

Worm wheels have 30 square teeth, setting circles 24 rim notches and worms seven plain rings; real tooth forms, threads and graduations are not modeled. The declination slow-motion rod runs along the polar X direction toward the eyepiece.
Tube, lens, eyepieces and finder are solid turned shapes (no optics); sleeves and rings have walls of 1.2 mm or more.
Shafts, pins and screws sit in bores 0.5 mm over their diameter, and sleeves, bands and brackets 0.6 mm over what they hold, so no two parts touch.

The parts list (bom: Korean and English names, materials, finishes, roles) is written for this example as if the user had handed it over with the sketch: materials and finishes follow brass-and-cast-iron instruments of the 1880s and are assumed, not read from the patent, and the listed sizes are the model's assumed sizes.
